Create a control library of 15 controls mapped to EU AI Act articles, NIST AI RMF subcategories and ISO 42001 Annex A, implement three as automated gates (eval report required, human-oversight config present, logging enabled), and generate an evidence pack per agent.

topics.title: EU AI Act for engineers
topics.explainer: Start with roles and classification: are you a provider or deployer, and is the system prohibited, high-risk, subject to transparency duties only, or minimal risk? Agents in employment, credit or essential-services decisions may be high-risk under Annex III. GPAI model providers have their own duties. Article 50 requires telling people they are interacting with AI and marking synthetic content. Track the amended timeline: Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027, Annex I from 2 August 2028. Always confirm interpretations with legal counsel.

subtopics.title: Provider vs deployer roles
subtopics.text: Providers develop or place AI systems on the market; deployers use them; obligations differ.

subtopics.title: Risk tiers and Annex III
subtopics.text: Annex III lists high-risk use areas such as employment, credit scoring and essential services.

subtopics.title: Article 50 transparency
subtopics.text: Article 50 requires telling people when they interact with AI and marking certain AI-generated content.

subtopics.title: Amended timeline (Omnibus 2026/1744)
subtopics.text: Application dates have been amended; always confirm the current timeline in the Official Journal or Commission guidance.

topics.title: NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001
topics.explainer: NIST AI RMF is voluntary and outcome-oriented: Govern sets culture, roles and policies; Map establishes context and risks; Measure assesses them with tests and metrics; Manage prioritizes and responds. The Generative AI Profile adds risks such as confabulation, information security and harmful content. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management system standard that can be certified, requiring an AI policy, risk and impact assessments, defined responsibilities, Annex A controls and continual improvement, structured like ISO 27001, so security teams recognize it.

subtopics.title: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
subtopics.text: NIST AI RMF's four functions: Govern (culture, roles), Map (context), Measure (assess), Manage (act on risks).

subtopics.title: ISO 42001 clauses and Annex A
subtopics.text: ISO/IEC 42001 has management-system clauses plus Annex A reference controls.

topics.title: Control libraries and crosswalks
topics.explainer: Write each control once in your own words, such as 'every production agent has a passing eval report less than 30 days old', then map it to the obligations it satisfies across frameworks. Assign an owner, an implementation (policy, gate, process), a test and an evidence source. The crosswalk shows coverage and gaps. Store it as data, not slides, so CI and dashboards can compute compliance status per agent and auditors can trace from obligation to evidence.

subtopics.title: Writing testable controls
subtopics.text: A testable control states a specific, checkable requirement, with how it's tested and how often.

subtopics.title: Crosswalk across frameworks
subtopics.text: A crosswalk maps each control to the requirements it satisfies in several frameworks.

subtopics.title: Coverage and gap analysis
subtopics.text: Find framework requirements that no control covers yet.

quiz.q: Under the amended EU AI Act, when do Annex III high-risk obligations apply?
quiz.why: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027.

quiz.q: What are the four functions of NIST AI RMF?
quiz.why: AI RMF core functions are Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

quiz.q: What distinguishes ISO/IEC 42001 from NIST AI RMF?
choices: It is a certifiable management system standard
quiz.why: ISO 42001 can be certified by accredited auditors; AI RMF is a voluntary framework.

lesson.intuition: Regulation becomes engineering when obligations turn into controls with owners, tests and evidence. The EU AI Act sets duties by role and risk level; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes risk work into Govern, Map, Measure and Manage; ISO/IEC 42001 defines a certifiable AI management system. A crosswalk lets one control satisfy several frameworks.
how: Determine your role (provider or deployer) and each system's risk tier under the EU AI Act, including high-risk use cases in Annex III and transparency duties.
Track the current application timeline from official sources, since dates have been amended.
Use NIST AI RMF functions (and its Generative AI Profile) to structure risk work; implement ISO/IEC 42001 as a management system aligned with ISO 27001.
Write testable controls with owners, tests and evidence sources.
Crosswalk controls to framework requirements, analyze gaps and drive dashboards from controls as data.
lesson.example: One control, three frameworks: control AI-07 'Every production model change passes the golden-set eval gate, with results retained 3 years'. Its test is a CI check plus quarterly sampling of 20 releases; its evidence is eval reports in the registry. It maps to NIST AI RMF Measure activities, ISO/IEC 42001 operational controls, and EU AI Act accuracy and record-keeping expectations for high-risk systems, so one test serves three audits.
mistakes: Treating regulations as a legal checklist with no engineering owner.
Controls like 'models are fair' that can't be tested.
Relying on secondary summaries for deadlines instead of official texts.
lesson.enterprise: A bank maintains 85 AI controls as YAML with owners, automated tests and evidence links. A crosswalk to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 shows 92% coverage; gaps become tickets with due dates.
takeaways: Obligations → controls → tests → evidence.
Know your role and risk tier; check official timelines.
Crosswalk once, satisfy many.

flowchart LR
  EU[EU AI Act] --> XW[Crosswalk]
  NIST[NIST AI RMF] --> XW
  ISO[ISO/IEC 42001] --> XW
  XW --> CTRL[(Controls as data: owner, test, evidence)]
  CTRL --> TEST[Automated tests]
  TEST --> EVID[(Evidence)]
  CTRL --> GAP[Gap analysis]
  EVID --> DASH[Dashboards + audits]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 feed a crosswalk into controls stored as data with owners, tests and evidence, driving automated tests, gap analysis and audit dashboards.

subjects.title: Agent Trajectory Evals and Simulation
subjects.why: Judging only the final answer misses agents that got lucky, wasted $20 on loops, or took a dangerous action along the way.
subjects.explainer:
Agent evals assess the whole trajectory: which tools were called, with what arguments, in what order, how many steps, at what cost, and whether any unsafe action was attempted. Final-state checks (is the ticket closed, is the database correct) are the most reliable signal; trajectory checks explain how it got there.

Techniques: environment-based evals with sandboxed tools and verifiable end states (SWE-bench style tests, τ-bench style simulated users and policies); trajectory assertions (required tools called, forbidden tools never called, step and cost budgets respected); LLM judges over traces for plan quality; and user simulators that role-play customers across many turns. Because agents are stochastic, run each task multiple times and report pass@k and pass^k (succeeds on all k tries), which exposes unreliability that a single run hides.

Common mistakes: grading by string-matching the final message; single runs per task; evaluating with mocked tools that never fail; ignoring cost and latency in scores.

Mental model: evaluate an agent like a new hire on a work sample: did they finish the job correctly, safely and efficiently, every time?

subjects.project: Build a sandbox environment for a customer-service agent with a mock order database, policy document and LLM user simulator. Create 40 tasks with verifiable end states and trajectory assertions. Run each task 5 times, report pass@1, pass^5, mean steps and cost, and show how one prompt change trades reliability against cost.

topics.title: End-state and trajectory checks
topics.explainer: Define success as a verifiable state of the environment: the right record updated, a test suite passing, a refund within policy. Add trajectory assertions for process requirements: identity verified before account changes, no forbidden tool calls, at most N steps, cost under budget. Store full traces so failures can be categorized: wrong tool, bad arguments, premature stop, loop, or policy violation. These categories map directly to fixes in prompts, tools or harness.

subtopics.title: Required and forbidden tool assertions
subtopics.text: Assert that certain tools were called (like verify_identity) and others never were (like delete_account).

subtopics.title: Step and cost budgets
subtopics.text: Fail runs that exceed a set number of steps or cost, even if they finish.

topics.title: Environments and user simulators
topics.explainer: Realistic evals need realistic environments: sandboxed APIs with seeded data, injected failures (timeouts, 500s, partial results) and policies. For conversational agents, an LLM user simulator with a persona and hidden goal plays the customer over many turns. Validate the simulator itself; unrealistic users produce misleading scores. Reset environments between runs so tasks are independent, and version environments alongside the agent.

subtopics.title: Fault injection
subtopics.text: Deliberately inject tool errors and timeouts to test recovery.

subtopics.title: Simulator validation
subtopics.text: Compare simulated conversations with real ones to make sure the simulator behaves realistically.

topics.title: Reliability metrics: pass@k and pass^k
topics.explainer: pass@k asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds, which suits tasks where a human picks the best attempt. pass^k asks whether all k attempts succeed, which is what matters for autonomous agents users rely on daily. An agent with 80% per-try success has pass^5 of about 33% if attempts are independent. Report both, plus variance in cost and steps. Reliability, not peak capability, is usually what blocks production deployment.

subtopics.title: pass@k definition
subtopics.text: pass@k is the chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds: 1 − (1 − p)^k for independent trials.

subtopics.title: pass^k for consistency
subtopics.text: pass^k is the chance that all k attempts succeed: p^k.

quiz.q: An agent succeeds 80% of the time per attempt, independently. What is pass^5 (all 5 succeed)?
Which is the most reliable success signal for an agent task?
choices: A verifiable end state of the environment
quiz.why: Checking the world state is objective.

quiz.q: Why inject tool failures in eval environments?
choices: Production tools fail; agents must handle errors gracefully
quiz.why: Mocks that never fail overestimate robustness.

lesson.intuition: Grading only an agent's final answer misses runs that got lucky, wasted money on loops, or did something dangerous along the way. Trajectory evals check the end state and the path: required and forbidden tool calls, step and cost budgets. Simulated environments and users make these tests repeatable, and pass^k measures whether the agent succeeds consistently.
how: Define verifiable end states (database rows, files, tickets) for each task.
Assert on the trajectory: required tools, forbidden tools, step and cost budgets; classify failures with a taxonomy.
Run in sandboxed, versioned environments with resets and fault injection (timeouts, errors).
Use LLM user simulators with goals for conversational tasks, validated against real users.
Run k independent trials per task and report pass@k, pass^k and cost and step variance.
lesson.example: pass@k vs pass^k with independent trials: per-trial success p = 0.8. pass@4 = 1 − 0.2⁴ = 99.84%. pass^4 = 0.8⁴ = 40.96%. If users run a task daily and need it to work every time, the 41% matters. Raising p to 0.95 gives pass^4 = 81.5%, showing how much per-run reliability drives consistency.
mistakes: Assuming a correct final answer means a correct process.
Testing against live systems that change between runs.
Using an unvalidated user simulator that's easier than real users.
lesson.enterprise: A telecom tests its billing-support agent on 120 simulated customer conversations, each run 5 times against a reset sandbox. Assertions forbid issuing credits without verification. It promotes autonomy only when pass^5 exceeds 80% and median cost stays under $0.40.
takeaways: Check end state and path.
Sandbox, reset, inject faults, validate simulators.
Report pass^k for consistency.

subjects.title: Agent Incident Response, Runbooks, Kill Switches and Cost Controls
subjects.why: Agents fail in new ways — loops, runaway spend, mass wrong actions — and operations needs pre-built levers to stop damage in seconds.
subjects.explainer:
An Agent Ops engineer prepares for incidents before they happen. Typical agent incidents: a model update degrades quality; a tool API changes and every call errors; an injection campaign; a loop that burns thousands of dollars per hour; mass incorrect write-backs; a provider outage.

Levers to build in advance: kill switches at several scopes (one tool, one agent, one tenant, all autonomous actions) controlled by feature flags and enforced by the gateway or policy engine; degrade modes (read-only, human-approval-required, fallback model); budget controls (per-run step and token caps, per-user and per-tenant daily spend limits, org-wide circuit breakers); and rollback for prompts, models and tool versions via registries and gateway aliases.

Runbooks document symptoms, dashboards, levers, communication and recovery for each scenario. Practice them in game days.

Common mistakes: no way to disable one tool without redeploying; spend alerts that fire after the monthly bill; rollbacks that revert code but not the prompt registry.

Mental model: every autonomous capability needs a brake pedal that works faster than the agent.

topics.title: Kill switches and degrade modes
topics.explainer: Design switches at multiple granularities so you can stop the smallest thing that fixes the problem. A tool switch disables refund_order everywhere; an agent switch pauses one agent; a tenant switch isolates one customer; a global autonomy switch forces approval mode for all write actions. Enforce switches outside the model, in the tool middleware or gateway, and make them take effect in seconds. Degrade modes keep service partly alive: read-only, approval required, or a smaller fallback model.

subtopics.title: Tool, agent, tenant, global switches
subtopics.text: Switches at different levels let you stop one tool or everything, matching the blast radius.

subtopics.title: Propagation latency targets
subtopics.text: Measure how fast a flip takes effect everywhere; aim for seconds.

topics.title: Budgets and cost controls
topics.explainer: Cost incidents are the most common agent incidents. Set per-run caps on steps, tokens and wall time; per-user and per-tenant daily spend limits; and an organization-wide circuit breaker on spend rate. Enforce through the LLM gateway with virtual keys and budgets, and stop runs gracefully with a clear message. Alert on cost per task trends and sudden spend spikes. Attribute every token to an agent, tenant and feature so finance and engineering can act on the same report.

subtopics.title: Spend-rate circuit breakers
subtopics.text: Trip automatically when spend rate exceeds a multiple of baseline for a set window.

subtopics.title: Gateway virtual keys
subtopics.text: Gateway virtual keys give each team or agent its own budget and limits.

topics.title: Runbooks, rollback and game days
topics.explainer: For each incident class write a runbook: detection signals and dashboards, first five minutes of actions, which switches to pull, who to page, customer communication, and recovery steps. Make rollback atomic across prompt, model alias, tool versions and policy bundle, recorded in a release manifest. Practice with game days that inject realistic failures. Blameless reviews should produce new alerts, tests and guardrails, not just a document.

subtopics.title: Runbook template
subtopics.text: A runbook lists symptoms, checks, actions, owners and communication steps for one incident type.

subtopics.title: Atomic release manifests and rollback
subtopics.text: A release manifest pins model, prompt, tools and policies together so rollback is one action.

subtopics.title: Game days
subtopics.text: Game days simulate failures so the team practices the runbook before a real incident.

quiz.q: A loop is burning $2,000/hour in one agent. What is the fastest correct lever?
choices: Flip that agent's kill switch / budget cap enforced at the gateway
quiz.why: Scoped kill switches and budgets stop damage in seconds.

quiz.q: Why enforce kill switches outside the model?
choices: A compromised or confused model cannot be trusted to obey
quiz.why: Enforcement must not depend on model compliance.

quiz.q: What makes a rollback complete for an agent release?
choices: Reverting prompt, model alias, tool versions and policies together
quiz.why: Agent behavior depends on all versioned components.

lesson.intuition: Agents fail in new ways: infinite loops, runaway spending, the same wrong action repeated thousands of times. Operations needs prepared levers that work in seconds: kill switches at several levels, degrade modes, hard budgets, spend-rate circuit breakers, and runbooks practiced in game days.
how: Build kill switches at tool, agent, tenant and global level, enforced in the gateway or middleware, with a propagation target in seconds.
Offer degrade modes: read-only, approval-only, fallback model.
Cap each run's steps, tokens and time; set per-user and per-tenant budgets via gateway virtual keys.
Add spend-rate circuit breakers and cost anomaly alerts with attribution.
Write runbooks, use atomic release manifests for rollback, practice game days and run blameless postmortems.
lesson.example: Spend-rate breaker: normal spend for an agent is about $40/hour. A breaker trips at 5× baseline sustained for 10 minutes. A bad prompt release causes loops that spend $250/hour (about $42 per 10 minutes). At 10 minutes the breaker switches the agent to approval-only mode; total excess spend is about $35 instead of $5,000+ if left running over a weekend (48 h × $210 excess ≈ $10,080).
mistakes: Kill switches that require a deploy to flip.
Budgets only at the monthly invoice level.
Runbooks that have never been rehearsed.
lesson.enterprise: A fintech's gateway enforces a global switch that disables all write tools within 5 seconds. In a quarterly game day, the team simulates a looping agent; the spend breaker trips, on-call follows the runbook and rolls back the release manifest in 4 minutes.
takeaways: Kill switches at every level, fast to flip.
Budgets per run, user and tenant; spend-rate breakers.
Practice with game days.

  BRK --> DEG[Degrade: read-only / approval-only / fallback model]
  KS --> RB[Runbook]
  DEG --> RB
  RB --> ROLL[Rollback release manifest]
  ROLL --> PM[Blameless postmortem]
lesson.diagramAlt: Diagram: an anomaly triggers breakers or alerts, leading to kill switches or degrade modes, followed by the runbook, rollback of the release manifest and a blameless postmortem.

subjects.title: Operating Agent Fleets 24/7
subjects.why: Enterprises are moving from a few copilots to hundreds of autonomous agents; running them like a fleet is a new operations discipline.
subjects.explainer:
A fleet is many agents, owned by many teams, sharing models, tools, data and budgets. Operating it needs a control plane: an agent registry (owner, purpose, risk tier, tools, data, versions, SLOs), standardized telemetry, shared gateways, central policy and budgets, and lifecycle management from proposal to retirement.

Risk tiers drive autonomy: low-risk agents act freely within budgets; medium-risk need sampling-based review; high-risk require approvals for actions and have stricter eval and audit requirements. Agent identity matters: each agent has its own identity and credentials so actions are attributable and revocable.

Fleet operations includes capacity planning across providers, model upgrade campaigns (re-evaluate every agent against the new model before switching aliases), cost governance (showback and chargeback), and inter-agent protocols such as A2A where agents delegate to each other, which adds new failure and trust paths.

Common mistakes: shadow agents nobody registered; one shared API key for all agents; model upgrades pushed fleet-wide without per-agent evals.

Mental model: treat agents like employees and services at once: each needs an identity, a manager, a job description, a budget and a performance review.

topics.title: Agent registry and lifecycle
topics.explainer: The registry is the source of truth: every agent has an ID, owner, business purpose, risk tier, declared tools and data products, model alias, prompt version, SLOs, budget and status. Gateways and policy engines consult it, so unregistered agents get no keys. Lifecycle stages run from proposal and review through pilot, production and retirement, with gates at each. The registry also feeds compliance inventories and cost reports.

subtopics.title: Registration as a gate for keys
subtopics.text: No registry entry, no credentials: this keeps shadow agents from running.

subtopics.title: Retirement and credential revocation
subtopics.text: Retiring an agent must revoke its identities and keys.

topics.title: Risk tiers, identity and autonomy
topics.explainer: Tier agents by the impact of their actions and data sensitivity. Tie autonomy levels to tiers: fully autonomous within budgets, sampled human review, or approval per action. Give each agent its own identity with scoped credentials, so its actions show up distinctly in audit logs and can be revoked alone. When agents call other agents, propagate the originating user and agent chain so authorization and accountability survive delegation.

subtopics.title: Autonomy levels per tier
subtopics.text: Higher-risk agents get less autonomy: more approvals, fewer write tools.

subtopics.title: Delegation chains and A2A
subtopics.text: When agents call other agents, record who delegated what to whom.

topics.title: Fleet-wide changes and economics
topics.explainer: Changes that affect many agents, such as a new model version, a shared tool upgrade or a policy change, need campaigns: run each agent's evals against the change, roll out progressively by tier, and keep per-agent rollback. Capacity planning spans providers and self-hosted models. Showback or chargeback attributes spend to owning teams, and fleet-level dashboards show value delivered per dollar, which is what executives fund.

subtopics.title: Model upgrade campaigns
subtopics.text: Upgrade campaigns move many agents to a new model, tracking each agent's eval results.

subtopics.title: Progressive rollout by tier
subtopics.text: Roll out to low-risk agents first, then higher tiers after monitoring.

subtopics.title: Showback and chargeback
subtopics.text: Showback reports cost to teams; chargeback actually bills them.

quiz.q: How should a fleet prevent unregistered 'shadow' agents?
choices: Make registry membership a precondition for gateway keys
quiz.why: Tying keys to registration enforces inventory.

quiz.q: Why give each agent its own identity?
choices: Attributable, scoped and individually revocable actions
quiz.why: Per-agent identity enables audit and targeted revocation.

quiz.q: Before switching the fleet to a new model version you should…
choices: Run each agent's evals and roll out progressively
quiz.why: Per-agent evaluation prevents fleet-wide regressions.

lesson.intuition: Enterprises are moving from a few copilots to hundreds of agents. Running them is like running a fleet: every agent is registered with an owner and risk tier, gets its own identity and an autonomy level matched to its risk, and changes like model upgrades roll out progressively by tier, with costs shown back to the teams that use them.
how: Keep an agent registry: purpose, owner, on-call, tools, data, risk tier, lifecycle stage.
Make registration the gate for getting credentials and model keys.
Tier agents by risk (data sensitivity, actions, audience) and set autonomy levels per tier.
Give each agent its own identity; track delegation chains, including agent-to-agent (A2A) calls; quarantine or revoke quickly.
Run fleet-wide campaigns (model upgrades) with progressive rollout by tier, capacity across providers, and showback of cost and value.
lesson.example: Model upgrade campaign: 240 agents must move to a new model before the old one is retired. Tier 3 (low risk, 150 agents) upgrades first after automated evals; tier 2 (70) follows after a week of monitoring; tier 1 (20, customer-facing actions) upgrades last with human review of eval diffs. 236 pass; 4 regress and stay pinned while owners fix prompts.
mistakes: Agents launched without registration or owner.
Same autonomy for every agent regardless of risk.
Retired agents whose credentials still work.
lesson.enterprise: A global insurer registers 310 agents. Registration issues gateway keys and workload identities; tier-1 agents need approval for payments; a monthly showback report lists cost and tasks completed per business unit.
takeaways: Registry = gate for credentials.
Risk tiers set autonomy.
Roll out fleet changes by tier; show back cost and value.
